metadata.title: Graph Reachability Pruning: Adaptive Data Reduction for Inexact Subgraph Matching
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper introduces Graph Reachability Pruning (GRP), a neighborhood-based data reduction algorithm for subgraph matching that outperforms existing methods. GRP automatically adapts a tolerance parameter to enable structurally inexact matching without requiring parameter tuning or a pre-computed index.

sections.heading: Reduction for Inexact Subgraph Matching
sections.text: Franklin Abodo STR Woburn, MA 01801, USA franklin.abodo@str.us Phillip Marvin STR Woburn, MA 01801, USA phillip.marvin@str.us Joanna Brown STR Woburn, MA 01801, USA joanna.brown@str.us Abstract —Subgraph matching is a fundamental graph analysis capability that many fields in science and technology depend on to retrieve information from data that are structured as graphs. These fields span network and cyber security, social and digital media, and the physical and life sciences. Because subgraph isomorphism is an NP-Complete problem, with depth-first search approaches having factorial time complexity and breadth-first approaches having factorial space complexity, efficient search space reduction is fundamental to the timely execution of queries against large, real world graphs having hundreds of millions or more nodes and edges. In this paper, we introduce Graph Reachability Pruning (GRP), a neighborhood-based data reduc- tion algorithm that discards all infeasible and many suboptimal regions of a knowledge graph prior to performing subgraph matching. The algorithm automatically adapts a missing neighbor tolerance parameter to enable structurally inexact matching without requiring cumbersome parameter tuning by an analyst and without relying on a space consuming pre-computed index. It outperforms the only known alternative algorithm, Inexact Local Constraint Checking (ILCC), which applies a single tolerance parameter uniformly across an entire query graph. In our real world case study, ILCC often fails to reduce knowledge graph data by more than a single digit percentage, whereas GRP often discards more than ninety-nine percent of the data. GRP operates independently from any search algorithm it might be paired with. Other data reduction methods are often integrated into, and operate concurrently with, a coupled search algorithm. This property of GRP gives it a versatility that is exceptionally useful. Index Terms —data reduction, space pruning, subgraph iso- morphism, approximate graph matching, greedy algorithm I. I NTRODUCTION Subgraph isomorphism is fundamental to a broad and di- verse array of pattern matching applications, from chem- and bio-informatics [1], [2], [3], to web and social network analysis [4], to cybersecurity [5], to digital media analysis [6]. As subgraph isomorphism is NP-Complete [7], applications in- volving large graphs with hundreds of millions or more nodes and edges require effective search space pruning techniques to manage the potentially factorial complexity [8]. The breadth of applications leads to a similar diversity of techniques for managing this complexity using various heuristic pruning and search ordering rules. For example, the foundational Ullmann’s algorithm [9] has been adapted several times in recent decades by introducing such heuristics [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. In this paper, we present a new search space reduction algo- rithm for structural and attributive inexact subgraph matching on large graphs with attribute-rich nodes and edges called Graph Reachability Pruning (GRP) 1 . GRP enables the ap- plication of time- and space-inefficient subgraph matching algorithms that exhaustively enumerate query graph (QG) matches to large knowledge graphs (KGs), like Ullmann’s and Maximally Discriminative Subgraph Matching (MDSM) [6], by fully discarding infeasible regions of the search space as well as many feasible regions that contain less structurally complete solutions. The two key innovations of GRP are 1) dynamic adaptation of a missing neighbor tolerance parameter in order to identify and preserve only the most structurally complete KG matches to QG neighborhoods, and 2) pruning of neighborhood edges in addition to nodes, allowing each reduction to influence pruning across the entire graph by requiring adjacent neighborhood connectivity. sections.heading: III. M
sections.text: ETHODS GRP is performed in two phases, one dedicated to attribute- based node and edge reduction, and a second dedicated to structure-based neighborhood reduction. Phase 1 constructs a data structure named the match graph, H, that maps QG nodes and edges to corresponding sets of similar KG nodes and edges. This is a coarse version of H that is later refined by neighborhood reduction in Phase 2. A. Node and Edge Reduction During construction of the match graph, KG nodes and edges are individually assigned to query node and edge mapping sets based on attribute similarity. A configuration file specifies the degree to which inexact similarity will be tolerated for each type of attribute, including categorical, nu- merical, Boolean, lexicographical, ranged, and Wikidata node identifiers [4]. The construction algorithm applies type-specific filters to each attribute, scores KG-to-QG match similarities based on per-attribute tolerances, and discards any KG element for which no QG element matches on all attributes given those scores and tolerances.
